title.en: There are no scores on this map

standfirst.en: Being on it is the verdict. Everything else here follows from that one decision.

clip.en: Three pins settling onto the map, filmed, photographed and written up, with no number on any of them.

en: The map opens on the places in Tallinn I have eaten at and would send a friend to. There is no rating on any of them, no stars, no mark out of ten, and there never will be. A place is either on the map or it is not, and that is the whole of the judgement this site makes.

A score sounds like more information and is usually less. Four point two against four point four tells you nothing about whether you will like the room, and a number invites the one question a recommendation should never have to answer: why is this one lower than that one? Leaving it out means the write-up has to do the work instead: what to order, what the place is like, who it is for.

One number does appear, and it is never mine. Google’s rating turns up on the places that are Google’s, and every time it does it says whose it is: according to Google, 4.8 from 3,041 reviews. Two kinds of claim about a restaurant, kept visibly apart.

What a pin says instead is what has been done about the place (filmed, photographed, or written up), and it says it by silhouette as well as by tone. Nothing on this site says something in colour alone.

title.en: Surprise me, with the map still under it

standfirst.en: The die picks from whatever the chips allow. On a phone it opens the place low, because the first thing you want back is not the write-up.

clip.en: The die on the rail pressed, and a place arriving in a sheet along the bottom with the pin it picked still lit above it.

en: The die on the left rail picks a place at random and opens it. It picks from whatever the filter chips currently allow, so choosing Korean and Cheap eats and then pressing it answers the question you were actually asking rather than a question about the whole city. Closed places are never offered, and the same place never comes back twice in a row.

On a phone it opens the sheet at its low stop rather than its full one, and that is the whole trick. A place you tapped by name opens at full height: you asked for that write-up, so the write-up is what you get. A surprise is the opposite errand. The name means nothing to you yet, and the first thing you want to know is whether it is round the corner or out in Lasnamäe, which is a question only the map can answer, and the sheet at full height was standing on it.
It sits on the rail rather than in the row of chips because that row scrolls sideways once the vocabulary gets wide, and a button that scrolls out of reach is no button at all.
Next to it is the speech bubble, which is the same button with the question turned round: one of them says anywhere, you choose, and the other says somewhere like this.

title.en: Up for a day and a half, and then gone

standfirst.en: A story is the one thing on this map that is not permanent. The picture in it stays all the same.

clip.en: The mark wearing a story’s turning ring while the hours left count down from thirty-six to none, and the ring going grey when they do.

en: Everything else here is a place that will still be there next year. A story is a video, or a photograph, that stands for a day and a half and then is not there any more, which is the entire reason anybody opens one now instead of later.

When something is up, the mark in the top left grows a turning ring, in this site’s own brick and ember rather than anybody else’s gradient. Press it and the story fills the screen: a bar along the top for each one, who it is from, how long it has left, the caption and a link. The left third of the screen goes back, the rest goes on, holding stops it, swiping down leaves.

The screen it fills is the one you can actually see and not the one the browser claims to have. Safari’s toolbar stands over the foot of an iPhone, and the caption and the link are precisely what ends up underneath it.

The video goes. The picture does not: the photograph a photo story was, or the still a video was watched from, moves onto the place it was shot at and joins that place’s photos. So the story is the moment, and the picture stays.

title.en: An account is a username and a password, and that is all of it

standfirst.en: No email, no phone, no real name, no sign in with anything. The smallest thing that does the job.

clip.en: A username and a password typed into the sign-up sheet, over the line saying a forgotten password cannot be recovered, and nothing else to fill in.

en: An account here holds a username, a password hash and, if you write one, a couple of hundred characters about yourself. There is no address field and no third party involved. That is not an oversight waiting to be fixed: it is the least of you that will make a list follow you to another phone, and anything past it would be a record of where somebody eats, kept for no reason anybody asked for.

It costs something, and the cost is said out loud rather than discovered. With no address on the account there is nowhere to send a reset, so a forgotten password cannot be recovered by anybody, including whoever runs this site. The sign-up sheet says that above the button, and the fields carry the hints that let a password manager keep the details, which is what actually rescues people.

There was a reset once: an optional address, a six-digit code, the lot. It was written, documented, and switched off in every deployment this site has ever had, because the mail it needed is not on the free plan. What it bought in practice was a paragraph promising something the site did not do. So it is gone, and the sentence about a lost password is now true in every configuration rather than in most of them.

Almost nothing is behind the account in any case. Saving works signed out. The one thing that genuinely needs it is a discount, because a restaurant giving something away is owed a person to count rather than a browser.

title.en: Google’s Tallinn is kept apart from mine, on purpose

standfirst.en: There is a second page with every place in the city on it. Nothing links to it, and that is the price of it existing at all.

clip.en: The same restaurant on two cards: the map’s write-up with no score, and the directory’s row carrying 4.5 and saying whose number that is.

en: Behind this site sits Google’s own export of everywhere in Tallinn you can eat or drink: names, ratings, review counts, price bands and opening hours, more than a thousand of them. It has a page of its own (searchable, filterable, with a map of the matches beside the list), and it is the single most useful thing here that is not a recommendation.

That is exactly why nothing points at it. Not the map, not the lists, not the sitemap; it asks search engines not to index it and the first paragraph on the page says, in every language the site speaks, that nothing on it has been visited and the ratings are Google’s. This site is one person’s description of a city and that page is a company’s, and a reader arriving from a search result would have no way to tell which one they had landed on.

The export is not left as Google wrote it. The category becomes cuisines this site can say in ten languages, the week becomes seven days with the day names taken off, and what survives untranslated is the times, the name of the restaurant and its street, which is what you would say to a taxi driver.

The most interesting thing a row on that page can say is On the map. That is the handful of places which are also in the catalogue here: a rating from one world and a write-up from the other, standing in the same card and clearly labelled.

title.en: The map is mine. A list is somebody else’s

standfirst.en: A name they chose, places they picked, a sentence about each one, and a link they can send to a friend.

clip.en: The third row of a list pressed, and a place landing in it with the sentence its author wrote about it.

en: Everything else on this site is one person’s opinion. A list is the other thing: top ten burgers, where to take your parents, the bakeries worth the walk. It carries the username of whoever wrote it, and it has an address they can paste into a message.

A list starts with three empty places, numbered, each a row you press to open the search. Three is where it starts because two places is a pair of opinions rather than a recommendation, and the search is over a much longer catalogue than the map: if the place you mean is not in it, you can add it yourself.

The address is the title plus six random characters, so the link says what it is before anybody opens it and cannot be guessed at from the one next to it. That random half is also what makes a private list private.

None of this touches the map. The pins, the write-ups and the filters are exactly what they were; lists live on their own pages, and the door to them is your own account page, filed under whoever you are. A list can be kept the way a place can be, and opened on the map as pins, which is the one place the two worlds meet.

title.en: The code you hold up at the table

standfirst.en: A discount is a QR code that changes every hour, a page for the waiter who scans it, and a link the restaurant bookmarks.

clip.en: A discount pass drawing itself: what is off the bill, the code for this hour, and the square a waiter scans.

en: A few places on the map give readers of it something off the bill. Which ones, and whether the offer is switched on at all, is one file. A place with nothing in that file is exactly the place it was before any of this existed.

The offer itself is not hidden from anybody: the pill on the row, the number in the panel, the words under the write-up and the Discount chip are drawn for everybody, because that is what somebody is deciding on. What takes an account is the code you hold up. This is the one thing on the site an account is genuinely for: saving works signed out, lists work signed out, a discount does not. And what it buys the restaurant is a person they can count rather than a browser.

The guest gets a QR code that is good for the hour. The waiter scans it and lands on a page that says yes or no, and the counter has a third page, bookmarked once, showing the code the guest’s screen is showing right now and the previous hour’s as well. That last one is the evening when the camera will not focus, the guest’s screen is cracked, or the cellar has no signal: comparing five characters by eye is slower than scanning and a great deal faster than turning somebody away.

A deal can also offer a rate it does not name. Give it a run (five to twenty-five percent, say) and every member who opens the pass is dealt one of them for the hour. The number runs through the whole range for a second and lands on theirs; reloading lands on the same one, and when the hour turns it is drawn again in front of them.

standfirst.en: Every list has said who wrote it since the day lists existed. The name was where the sentence stopped.

clip.en: The byline under a list pressed, and the page behind it arriving: everything else that person published, and how often it was kept.

en: Press a name on a list now and you get that person: the public lists they have made, newest first, how many places are on each and how many people kept it, the year they turned up, one number over the lot saying how often in all their lists have been kept, and the line they wrote about themselves, if they wrote one.

That is the whole of it, and the omissions are the design. Not their saves: those are anonymous by intent and filed under a device as often as under an account, and a page that turned them into a public record of where somebody eats would be a different site altogether. Not a follower count, because there is nothing here to follow.

The page is not a second page. It is the same file the lists are served from, handed back at another address with that person’s own title and preview card written into it, so a link somebody pastes into a chat arrives as who it is rather than as a bare blue URL. There is no second stylesheet and no second boot.

Everybody’s lists are gathered in one place too, most-kept first, with a field to search them, which is what makes a list something a stranger can find, rather than something that travels only by the link its author remembers to send.

title.en: Ask for somewhere, in a sentence

standfirst.en: Cheap asian food. Somewhere for a date. Khachapuri, still open. The panel answers with places, and it remembers what you asked a minute ago.

clip.en: A sentence typed into the chat (cheap asian food, still open) becoming a turn in the thread, with two places under the answer.

en: The speech bubble opens the panel on a chat, and the site speaks first: what do you feel like? Type a sentence and it sits on the right the way your own words do in any chat, with the answer under it: a line or two, then one to three places as rows, best first, each with a reason it is there and, when the map knows where you are, how far it is.

It is a conversation and the model is told the whole of it. Every question goes with the exchanges before it, so somewhere cheaper, or is the second one open late, mean what they would mean to a person. One place is a whole answer when one is what fits: a model asked for three will always find three.

It answers off my map first, the places I have eaten at and written up, and reaches for Google’s Tallinn only where the map has nothing that fits: a cuisine I have not got to yet, a part of town I have not eaten in. A place off Google’s list arrives wearing Google’s name and rating and none of my words, and says so. There used to be a choice to make before typing, this map or all of Tallinn; nobody opening a chat wants to be asked which of two maps they mean, so there is one Ask now.

It runs on a free daily allowance, and some evenings that allowance is gone. When it is, the chat says so and asks you back tomorrow rather than guessing: three places matched on letters under a sentence about your evening would be the site pretending, and a shrug is honest where that is not.

title.en: The station follows you off the map

standfirst.en: One button, one stream, and it keeps playing while you walk from the map to a list.

clip.en: The radio button pressed: the pill takes the station’s name and the bars beneath it start moving.

en: There is a radio on the rail. It plays one station for everybody and, where there is one, a station per language, so the site can be read in Ukrainian with Ukrainian rock behind it, and a language with no station of its own falls back to the shared one rather than to silence.

Switching language while it is playing switches the station under it, instead of leaving the old one running behind a button that now names a different one. Doing that a second after pressing play, while the stream is still connecting, is the same switch, and getting that right took more care than the feature deserved: the interrupted connection reports a failure that is the site’s own doing, and for a while it was read as the stream refusing to start. The radio would turn itself off, with a message saying so, over a station that had in fact started.
It is the same button on every page that has one, so the music does not stop because you walked from the map to somebody’s list. And it is one file: empty it and the button never appears at all.

title.en: Where to eat in Tallinn, from somebody who has eaten there

standfirst.en: Every place on one map is somewhere I have eaten. How to use it, neighbourhood by neighbourhood, and where the lists come in.

en: Search for where to eat in Tallinn and you get the same twenty places ranked by the same stars. This site is the other way round: [a map](/) of the places I have eaten at myself and would send a friend to, with no score on any of them. Being on the map is the verdict, and [why there are no scores](/blog?post=no-scores-on-this-map) is a post of its own.

In the Old Town, the walls hide more than tourist menus. [Pulla Bakery](/?spot=pulla-bakery) bakes sourdough buns in a room that feels like a living room, [Koht](/?spot=koht) keeps more than 800 beers behind a small door on Lai, [Izakaya Taro](/?spot=izakaya-taro) does Japanese small plates on Müürivahe, and [MIX Resto](/?spot=mix-resto) serves a three-course lunch for twenty euro. [Vegan Restoran V](/?spot=vegan-restoran-v) has been on Rataskaevu for years, and [Veino](/?spot=veino) is a small wine bar a few doors down, run by people who know every bottle on the shelf.

Telliskivi and Kalamaja are where most of an ordinary week happens. [F-Hoone](/?spot=f-hoone) for breakfast or pelmeni, [Põhja Konn](/?spot=pohja-konn) for Põhjala's beer on a balcony, [The Brick Coffee Roastery](/?spot=the-brick-coffee) for a date, [Kartul](/?spot=kartul) for a fully vegan stuffed potato by the tram stop, and [Xinhai 1911](/?spot=xinhai-1911) by Balti jaam for biang biang noodles, one noodle metres long in chili oil.

In Kadriorg, [Radio](/?spot=radio-restoran) is for sharing whatever is on the menu, [Faehlmanni kohvik](/?spot=faehlmanni-kohvik) is brunch on one of the nicest corners in the neighbourhood, and [Magussoolane](/?spot=magussoolane) is a bakery I only found because of the smell. On the Noblessner waterfront, [180° by Matthias Diether](/?spot=180-degrees) is the only two Michelin star restaurant in the Baltics, and [KotKot](/?spot=kotkot) is the chicken burger for every other night.

Some of the best cooking in the city is fifteen minutes from any postcard. [Annön](/?spot=annon) does Soviet Korean comfort food in Lasnamäe, [Varkizana](/?spot=varkizana) is a Greek tavern out there too, [DVIN](/?spot=dvin) makes khinkali in Kopli at prices you will not believe, and [Crustum Bakery](/?spot=crustum-bakery) has been feeding Mustamäe for years.

The chips along the top of the map narrow it down: [bakeries](/?type=bakery), [beer](/?type=pub), [cheap eats](/?type=cheap-eats), [hidden gems](/?type=hidden-gem), [somewhere to bring a laptop](/?type=laptop). Every place opens on what to order, which is the question you actually have once you are through the door.

The map is one person's. For everybody else's there are [lists](/lists): [Google's top ten restaurants in Tallinn](/list/top-ten-restaurants-by-google-pt7mwk), worked out from its reviews, and lists people wrote under their own names, like [the tallinneats top thirty](/list/top-30-places-in-tallinn-zdmz94). The posts after this one go through them kind by kind: [Google's top tens](/blog?post=top-restaurants-in-tallinn-by-google), [bakeries and coffee](/blog?post=bakeries-and-coffee-in-tallinn), [craft beer](/blog?post=craft-beer-in-tallinn), [cheap eats](/blog?post=cheap-eats-in-tallinn) and [Georgian and Azerbaijani food](/blog?post=georgian-and-azerbaijani-food-in-tallinn).

title.en: The top restaurants in Tallinn, by Google, and how the ranking works

standfirst.en: Six lists worked out from Google’s own reviews: restaurants, bakeries, cafés, bars, pizzerias, and twenty places over all of them.

en: The one word this map will not say is best. Google will, and it has a city's worth of reviews to say it with, so the site keeps six lists that are Google's verdict rather than mine, each under Google's name: [the top ten restaurants](/list/top-ten-restaurants-by-google-pt7mwk), [the top ten bakeries](/list/top-ten-bakeries-by-google-65nfrf), [the top ten cafés](/list/top-ten-cafes-by-google-jz7c2b), [the top ten bars](/list/top-ten-bars-by-google-8y6grz), [the top ten pizzerias](/list/top-ten-pizzerias-by-google-k83p93) and [the top twenty over everything](/list/top-twenty-places-by-google-kwb7l5).

The rating is weighed by how many people gave it. A 4.5 from five thousand reviews outranks a 4.7 from sixty, and a place with fewer than a hundred reviews is not counted at all, because a perfect score from a dozen friends is not the same claim as a 4.8 from a city.

At the top of the restaurants, as this is written, is Restaurant Rataskaevu 16, which the tallinneats list sums up as a medieval room and a kitchen that takes elk seriously. Then [Vegan Restoran V](/?spot=vegan-restoran-v), [Saffron](/?spot=saffron), Väike-Rataskaevu, Restoran Mimosa, The Kurze, [Ramen Taro](/?spot=ramen-taro), Pizzeria Santa Lucia, Osteria Moderna and [MIX](/?spot=mix-resto).

Several of those are on my map as well, which is about the overlap you would expect between a city's average and one person's week. Where the two agree, go. Where they do not, it is usually because Google's list is full of places a lot of people visit once, and mine is full of places I go back to.

The bakeries list is the one I argue with least. [Pulla Bakery](/?spot=pulla-bakery) is at the top, then [Crustum](/?spot=crustum-bakery), RØST, [Bruto Bakehouse](/?spot=bruto-bakehouse) and [Buxhöwden](/?spot=buxhowden-pagar), with [Magussoolane](/?spot=magussoolane) and [La Boulangerie](/?spot=la-boulangerie) further down. [The post about bakeries](/blog?post=bakeries-and-coffee-in-tallinn) goes through them.

The bars list leans towards cocktails and wine (Toro, Whisper Sister, Botaanik, Vixen Vinoteek), with [Koht](/?spot=koht) the one beer bar in its top five. For beer on its own terms, [the post about craft beer](/blog?post=craft-beer-in-tallinn) is the other half.

The lists are worked out again whenever the site's copy of Google's places is refreshed, so the order moves. The address does not: every one of them is a page you can send somebody, with a line under each place saying what Google's rating was and how many people gave it.

title.en: Bakeries and coffee in Tallinn: cinnamon buns, kringel and a Saturday croissant

standfirst.en: The bakeries on the map, the two lists that argue with it, and where to sit with a coffee for a morning.

en: Tallinn is a bakery city, and the map shows it: press [Bakery](/?type=bakery) along the top and see how much of the map is still standing.

In the Old Town, [Pulla Bakery](/?spot=pulla-bakery) on Voorimehe is handmade sourdough buns baked by a mother and daughter, and the cinnamon bun is the thing to order. On the same street, [Karu Talu Šokolaad](/?spot=karu-talu-sokolaad) makes three hundred family-size cookies on the days it is open, and when they are gone they are gone. [Bruto Bakehouse](/?spot=bruto-bakehouse) on Suur-Karja lives for cookies too, and the pistachio one is the favourite.

[François Boulangerie](/?spot=francois-boulangerie) is the one you plan for: Saturdays only, ordered in advance, collected from a queue outside the house on Härjapea. [La Boulangerie](/?spot=la-boulangerie) is the everyday version, with a pistachio roll worth crossing town for, and [Crustum](/?spot=crustum-bakery) in Mustamäe is where the same team started.

Kringel is the Estonian twisted loaf, and two places make it worth seeking out: [Bekker Pagariäri](/?spot=bekker-pagariari) in Kopli, the old bakery that supplies bread and kringel to lots of places in town, where the salted caramel one is ridiculous, and [Kringel](/?spot=kringel) in Uus Maailm, which is vegan and hugely popular for good reason.

For coffee, [Paper Mill Coffee](/?spot=paper-mill-coffee) is in a fire station built in 1912 and counts among the top thirty speciality coffee shops in Europe, and [its second shop in Volta](/?spot=paper-mill-coffee-volta) is where the monkey bread is. [The Brick](/?spot=the-brick-coffee) roasts its own in Telliskivi, [Kokomo](/?spot=kokomo) on Ankru is the cosiest room going, and [Värav](/?spot=varav-coffee-toast) is a little white house under the Old Town bastion. For tea rather than coffee, [Chamber Tea](/?spot=chamber-tea) and [Morii Tea House](/?spot=morii-tea-house).

Then the two lists that do not quite agree with me. [Google's top ten bakeries](/list/top-ten-bakeries-by-google-65nfrf) puts Pulla at the top as well, and adds RØST, Mathilda on the Hill and Kalamaja Bakery, which are not on the map yet. [The top ten coffee, tea and bakery](/list/top-10-bakery-bwvp2x) by [etibar](/u/etibar) is one person's Saturday morning instead: François first, then Pulla, The Brick, Fotografiska's café, Paper Mill Volta and Porgandipomm, with Põhjala's taproom slipped in because a list is allowed its opinions.

And for somewhere to stay with a book, [the best places to read a book](/list/best-places-to-read-book-7t76c8) by [qarin-qulu](/u/qarin-qulu) picks by the chairs: Chamber Tea, Kokomo, a chocolate shop and a bookshop café in Telliskivi.

title.en: Craft beer in Tallinn: taprooms, 800 bottles and the cheapest pint in the centre

standfirst.en: Where the beer is good, from Põhjala’s own bar to a sauna in the city wall.

en: Estonian craft beer punches well above the size of the country, and Tallinn is where to drink it. Press [Beer/pub](/?type=pub) on the map and these are the places left.

[Põhja Konn](/?spot=pohja-konn) is Põhjala's own bar in Telliskivi, pouring their beers next to plenty of other craft; take the balcony if it is free. [Tuletorn](/?spot=tuletorn) on Ankru is brewers from Põhjala who set out to make something better, and nailed it.

[Koht](/?spot=koht) on Lai has more than 800 kinds of beer: start light, work up through the IPAs, finish on a stout. [Mikkeller](/?spot=mikkeller-old-town) on Kullassepa pairs one of the biggest names in craft beer with a kitchen run by Viljandi Burger. [Hell Hunt](/?spot=hell-hunt) on Pikk pours Humalakoda, and the fish and chips hold up.

[Pühaste Taproom](/?spot=puhaste-taproom) in Rotermann is a Tartu brewery whose double IPAs are the reason to come. [Vaat](/?spot=vaat-brewery) is a brewery and taproom well out in Paljassaare, reachable by bus or by bike. And [Laboratooriumi 23](/?spot=laboratooriumi-23) is foosball, sandwiches, craft beer and a sauna in one place by the city wall; finding it is half of it.

For the cheaper end, [Uba ja Humal](/?spot=uba-ja-humal) has the cheapest beer in the centre, over twenty taps and a kebab from next door. [Vana Villem](/?spot=vana-villem) is a cozy local pub, open late every day. [Pilsneri baar](/?spot=pilsneri-baar) pours Pilsner Urquell three different ways in a garden, and [Pudel](/?spot=pudel) in Telliskivi is where to take a group for the evening.

[Best beer bars](/list/top-bars-hxzz7m), the list this site keeps under [its own name](/u/tallinntastebuds), puts eight of those in an order with a line on each: Põhjala Brewery's taproom for its American barbecue, Koht for the 800, Uba ja Humal for the prices. [Google's top ten bars](/list/top-ten-bars-by-google-8y6grz) is a different city altogether, cocktails and wine, with Koht the one beer bar near the top.

title.en: Cheap eats in Tallinn that are not a compromise

standfirst.en: Khinkali, a stuffed potato, a twenty-euro lunch menu, and a kebab worth the ride out.

en: Eating out in Tallinn is not cheap any more, which is why the map has a [Cheap eats](/?type=cheap-eats) chip. Everything under it is somewhere I would go even if it cost more.

[DVIN](/?spot=dvin) in Kopli is honest Georgian food at prices you would not believe: khinkali, shashlik, and a napoleon cake to finish. [Annön](/?spot=annon) in Lasnamäe cooks Soviet Korean comfort food (beef heart salad, lamb soup) on the principle that food should be useful to the body.

[Kartul](/?spot=kartul) by the Telliskivi tram stop is fully vegan and built entirely around the potato: stuffed baked potatoes and homemade dumplings. [Burger Box](/?spot=burger-box) on Kopli started as a small burger window and kept its street-food soul, with kimchi fries, cheese balls and laksa. [KotKot](/?spot=kotkot) at Noblessner is the chicken burger.

[MIX Resto](/?spot=mix-resto) is the one that sounds wrong: fine dining in the Old Town, at a three-course lunch menu for twenty euro that changes with the seasons. [Pulla Bakery](/?spot=pulla-bakery) is a cinnamon bun and a coffee for very little.

[Shaurma Kebab Linnamäe](/?spot=shaurma-kebab-linnamae) is a Turkish kebab counter out in Linnamäe, and worth every penny. For drinks, [Uba ja Humal](/?spot=uba-ja-humal) has the cheapest beer in the centre, [Vana Villem](/?spot=vana-villem) big portions and cheap beer until late, and [Vabrik](/?spot=vabrik) the cheapest wine in town, with a bottle shop to take one home from.

title.en: Georgian and Azerbaijani food in Tallinn: khinkali, plov and qutab

standfirst.en: The Caucasian kitchens on the map, from somebody who grew up on the food.

en: I am from Azerbaijan, so this is the part of the map I am hardest to please about. Press [Caucasian](/?type=caucasian) and these are the ones that passed.

[Badam](/?spot=badam), next to the bus station, is the most authentic Azerbaijani cooking in Tallinn: küftə, dolma, xangal, piti and plov, lamb plov included. [Faeton](/?spot=faeton) on Köleri serves proper Azerbaijani cuisine beyond the shashlik, and its qutab has a twist that works, filled with greens and mozzarella, with ayran to drink.

For Georgian, [Gobi](/?spot=gobi) in Rotermann is the modern version, and the adjaruli khachapuri and the khinkali are why you go back. [Pirosmani](/?spot=pirosmani) on Tartu maantee is big on flavour and generous in size, made for sharing: chashushuli, adjarian khachapuri, khinkali. [DVIN](/?spot=dvin) in Kopli is the honest, cheap one, with a napoleon cake to finish.

Two more for the grill: [Baklažaan](/?spot=baklazaan), out on the way to the Nõmme bike route, for shashlik, and [Telliskivi Šašlõkk](/?spot=telliskivi-saslokk), which is really Turkish, bakes its own bread, and does a lahmajun worth ordering.
And if the menu in front of you is in Estonian rather than Georgian, [the flashcards](/flashcard) have a deck for [at the table](/flashcard?d=table).
